title: Distributed cache failure modes
scopeHtml:
Scope: stampede, penetration, avalanche, hot keys, Redis Cluster hash slots, Memcached vs Redis.

Scope: stampede, penetration, avalanche, hot keys, Redis Cluster hash slots, Memcached vs Redis.

notes.title: Cache stampede (thundering herd)
notes.html:
A stampede happens when a hot key expires and thousands of requests all miss at once, all hit the database for the same value. The database was sized for a 95% hit ratio and suddenly sees 100% for that key.

Worked example. A homepage key serves 20,000 reads/s. Rebuilding it takes 800 ms of heavy SQL. At expiry, for 800 ms about 16,000 requests all miss and all run the query: 16,000 concurrent heavy queries. The DB saturates, the rebuild slows, more requests pile up, and it can spiral into an outage.

Fixes:

  1. Single-flight / lock: the first misser takes a lock (SET lock:key id NX PX 5000), rebuilds, others wait briefly or serve stale.
  2. Stale-while-revalidate: store a soft TTL inside the value; after it, serve the old value while one worker refreshes in the background.
  3. Probabilistic early refresh: each reader refreshes slightly before expiry with rising probability, so refresh happens before the cliff.
  4. Refresh by a scheduled job for the handful of known hot keys.

Decision gravity. Locks add a failure mode (a crashed holder), so always use a lock TTL. Stale-while-revalidate is the cheapest to adopt and is reversible. It breaks for data that must be exactly fresh.

Industry examples. Facebook's Memcache "leases" hand one client the right to refill a key. Go's singleflight and Caffeine's refreshAfterWrite do this in-process. CDNs offer stale-while-revalidate and request collapsing.

Everyday analogy. The shop runs out of bread at 8 am and 200 people shout at the baker at once; better that one person asks the baker and everyone waits at the counter.

Common interview traps.

  • Lock with no expiry; a crash then blocks the key forever.
  • Waiters polling in a tight loop. Use a short sleep with jitter.
  • Only protecting against one process; you need it cross-server too, or at least per-server collapsing.

notes.title: Cache penetration
notes.html:
Penetration is requests for keys that do not exist anywhere, so every one misses the cache and hits the DB. Normal caching cannot help because there is nothing to cache. Causes: bugs, scrapers guessing IDs (/user/99999999), or attackers.

Defences:

  • Cache negative results with a short TTL (30 to 60 s): store a NULL marker.
  • Bloom filter of all valid IDs in front of the DB: if the filter says "definitely not present", reject without any lookup. False positives are possible, false negatives are not.
  • Input validation (ID format and range) and rate limiting per IP.

Worked example. 100M valid user IDs in a Bloom filter at 1% false-positive rate need about 9.6 bits per item, so around 120 MB. An attacker sending 50,000 random-ID requests/s gets 99% rejected in memory; only about 500/s reach the DB.

Industry examples. Redis Stack offers Bloom filter commands (RedisBloom). Chrome used a Bloom-filter style check for malicious URLs. Cassandra and HBase use Bloom filters per SSTable to skip disk reads.

Everyday analogy. A receptionist with the guest list rejecting anyone not on it, instead of phoning every office.

Common interview traps.

  • Negative caching with a long TTL: a newly created record looks missing.
  • A Bloom filter that cannot delete; plan for rebuilds or a counting variant.

notes.title: Cache avalanche
notes.html:
An avalanche is many keys expiring at the same time, or the whole cache dying, so the database takes the full load at once. A stampede is one hot key; an avalanche is many keys or the whole cache.

Typical causes: a batch job loaded 1M keys with TTL 3600, so they all vanish at the same minute; or a Redis node restarts empty.

Fixes:

  • TTL jitter: ttl = base + random(0, 0.2 * base).
  • Multi-layer cache: a small in-process cache (Caffeine, 30 s) in front of Redis softens a Redis outage.
  • Replicas and clustering so one node loss does not empty everything; Redis Sentinel or Cluster failover.
  • Load shedding / circuit breakers on the DB path so the DB degrades gracefully.
  • Warm-up a new cache before moving traffic.
ttl = 3600 + random.randint(0, 600)   # spreads expiry over 10 minutes
redis.set(key, val, ex=ttl)

Industry examples. Public postmortems of cache-flush outages follow this pattern: the cache cold starts and the DB falls over. Hotstar-style live events pre-warm caches before the match starts.

Everyday analogy. Every ticket-counter clerk takes lunch at exactly 1 pm; stagger the breaks.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing "Redis is fast" removes the need for DB capacity planning. The DB must survive a cold cache at a degraded rate.
  • Fixing TTLs but not the cold-start path.

notes.title: Hot keys and big keys
notes.html:
A hot key is one key receiving far more traffic than one cache node can handle. In a sharded cache, hashing puts that key on a single node, so adding nodes does not help. A big key is a single huge value (a list with 5M entries) that blocks the single-threaded Redis event loop on every access.

Worked example. A celebrity profile gets 300,000 reads/s. One Redis node handles roughly 100,000 simple ops/s. That node saturates while the other 9 are idle.

Fixes:

  • Local in-process cache for the hot key (even 1 s TTL cuts Redis load by nearly 100% for that key).
  • Key splitting / replication: store profile:42#0..#9 copies, read a random one (10 nodes share the load). Writes must update all copies.
  • Read replicas for the shard.
  • Detect first: Redis --hotkeys (needs an LFU policy) or redis-cli --bigkeys, client-side counters, and sampled monitoring.
  • Break big keys into pieces (hash of buckets), use UNLINK instead of DEL for async free.

Industry examples. Twitter handled celebrity tweets with replicated and local caching; Instagram and Alibaba use client-side hot-key detection with local caches.

Everyday analogy. One popular dish served from one stove: add stoves, or cook a batch ahead and put copies on every counter.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "add more shards" for a single hot key. Sharding does not split one key.
  • Running KEYS * or DEL on a huge key in production; it blocks.

notes.title: Redis Cluster and hash slots
notes.html:
Redis Cluster splits the key space into 16,384 hash slots; each master owns a range of slots. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384. A client learns the slot map and talks to the right node directly. If it asks the wrong node it gets MOVED slot host:port.

Example layout for 3 masters: A owns 0 to 5460, B owns 5461 to 10922, C owns 10923 to 16383, each with 1 replica. Adding a node means moving slots (live resharding), not rehashing everything, which is why there is no big one-way migration. Failover: if a master is unreachable for cluster-node-timeout (for example 15000 ms), a replica is promoted.

Multi-key commands only work when all keys are in the same slot. Use hash tags: {user42}:cart and {user42}:profile hash only the part in braces, landing together. Overusing one tag makes a hot slot.

redis-cli --cluster create h1:6379 h2:6379 h3:6379 h4:6379 h5:6379 h6:6379 --cluster-replicas 1

Gravity. Picking cluster vs one big instance: a single node with replicas and Sentinel is simpler up to roughly 25 to 100 GB and about 100k ops/s. Cluster is needed beyond a node's RAM or throughput. Moving from single to cluster means client and key-design changes (multi-key ops), so it is semi one-way.

Industry examples. Twitter ran huge Redis/Twemproxy fleets; Redis Cluster is used by many; managed options include ElastiCache cluster mode and Redis Enterprise. Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose acknowledged recent writes.

Everyday analogy. A library split into 16,384 shelves, each librarian responsible for a range of shelves, with a map at the door.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking Redis Cluster gives strong consistency; replication is async.
  • Forgetting MULTI and Lua scripts need same-slot keys.
  • Saying keys are hashed to nodes directly; it is keys to slots to nodes.

notes.title: Memcached vs Redis
notes.html:
Memcached is a simple, multi-threaded string cache. Redis is a single-threaded-per-command data structure server with optional persistence.

Memcached Redis
Data types Strings only Strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLog
Threads Multi-threaded (uses many cores per node) Command execution single-threaded (I/O threads since 6.0)
Persistence None RDB snapshots, AOF log
Replication/HA None built in (client-side sharding) Replicas, Sentinel, Cluster
Eviction LRU Several policies incl. LFU
Extras Very low overhead per key Pub/sub, Lua, transactions, TTL per key, geo

Choose Memcached for a pure, huge, simple key/value cache where multi-core use and low per-item overhead matter. Choose Redis when you need counters, leaderboards (sorted sets), rate limiters, queues, locks, or persistence and failover. Today most teams pick Redis; Memcached remains at Facebook scale and in some legacy stacks. Choice is reversible if you only use get/set behind an interface.

Worked example. A leaderboard of 5M players: Redis ZADD and ZREVRANGE 0 99 in O(log N). In Memcached you would fetch and sort in app code.

Industry examples. Facebook (Memcached at huge scale), Twitter (both), Pinterest, Snapchat (Redis), Netflix (EVCache is Memcached-based).

Everyday analogy. Memcached is a plain sticky-note board; Redis is a small toolbox with a drawer system.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "Redis is faster" with no context. On big multi-core boxes Memcached can serve more throughput for plain gets.
  • Treating Redis as a durable database without understanding AOF appendfsync everysec can lose about 1 s of writes.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Stampede = one hot key expires: use single-flight locks (with TTL), stale-while-revalidate, early refresh.
  • Penetration = keys that never exist: cache negatives briefly, Bloom filter, validation, rate limits.
  • Avalanche = mass expiry or cache loss: TTL jitter, layered caches, replicas, DB load shedding, warm-up.
  • Hot keys do not shard away: local cache, key copies, detect with LFU and --hotkeys; split big keys.
  • Redis Cluster: 16,384 slots, CRC16 mod 16384, MOVED, hash tags, async replication.
  • Memcached for simple multi-threaded caching; Redis for rich types, persistence and HA.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between cache stampede, penetration and avalanche, and what is the first fix for each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These terms get mixed up; the answer shows you diagnose by symptom.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Stampede: one hot key expires and thousands of requests rebuild it at once; fix with single-flight or stale-while-revalidate. Penetration: requests for keys that exist nowhere, so every one reaches the DB; fix with negative caching and a Bloom filter. Avalanche: many keys expire together or the whole cache dies; fix with TTL jitter, replicas, layered caches and warm-up.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Failure       Trigger                     Shape of DB load            First fix
Stampede      1 hot key expires           spike of N identical queries single-flight / SWR
Penetration   key absent everywhere       steady, never ends          negative cache, Bloom
Avalanche     mass expiry / cache loss    wide spike, many keys       jitter, replicas, warm-up

The common thread: the DB was sized for the miss rate of a healthy cache. Each failure mode is a way the miss rate jumps. The DB protections (load shedding, circuit breaker, connection limits) are the last line for all three.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using "avalanche" for a single hot key.
  • Fixing TTL jitter but not the cold-start path.
  • Treating penetration as a cache problem when it is an input-validation problem.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which one never clears on its own? -> Penetration; the keys never become cacheable.
  2. Which is cheapest to fix? -> TTL jitter, one line.
  3. How would a DB circuit breaker help? -> It caps concurrent DB calls and returns stale or default data instead of queueing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: definitions. Senior: symptom shapes in graphs, plus the DB-side protection that covers all three.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flash sale ran all three in one night: a hot key expired, a scraper probed IDs, and a node restart cleared a shard.

questions.promptHtml: How does Redis Cluster decide which node owns a key, and what happens when a client asks the wrong node?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know "keys to slots to nodes" and its consequences for multi-key ops and resharding.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The key space is 16,384 hash slots. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each master owns a range of slots. The client caches the slot map and talks to the owner directly. A wrong node replies MOVED slot host:port and the client refreshes its map. Adding a node moves slots, not every key.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
3 masters: A 0-5460   B 5461-10922   C 10923-16383, each with 1 replica
key -> CRC16 -> slot 7000 -> master B (replica B' on failover)

Resharding migrates slots live; during migration a client may get ASK for keys already moved. Multi-key commands, MULTI and Lua need all keys in one slot, or the server returns CROSSSLOT. Hash tags {user42}:cart hash only the braces. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover after cluster-node-timeout can lose recent acknowledged writes. Cluster is not strongly consistent.

redis-cli --cluster create h1:6379 h2:6379 h3:6379 h4:6379 h5:6379 h6:6379 --cluster-replicas 1
redis-cli -c -h h1 cluster keyslot "{user42}:cart"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Keys hash to nodes", forgetting slots.
  • Using one hash tag for a whole tenant: one hot slot.
  • Assuming cluster failover never loses writes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why 16,384 slots? -> Small enough that the slot bitmap in gossip stays compact, large enough to balance up to about 1,000 masters.
  2. MOVED vs ASK? -> MOVED is permanent ownership; ASK is a one-time redirect during migration.
  3. When is a single node better? -> Below roughly 25-100 GB and ~100k ops/s, with replicas and Sentinel, since it avoids key-design limits.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it shards keys". Senior: slots, MOVED/ASK, CROSSSLOT, async replication loss and the single-node alternative.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migration to cluster failed on day one because a Lua script touched keys in two slots.

questions.contextHtml: Every day at about 10:00:00 the home page latency spikes from 40 ms to 6 s for 20 seconds; DB CPU hits 100%. The home page JSON is cached under home:v3 with EX 600, written by a cache-aside loader. Traffic: 20,000 reads/s on that key. The loader runs a 900 ms aggregation query. Slow query log shows 15,000+ identical copies of the aggregation at 10:00:00. Red herring: a deploy happened at 09:50.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the TTL" or "scale the DB". Both delay the cliff without removing it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the key rebuilt by one writer or by every request? Why 10:00 exactly: the TTL expires 600 s after a refill that started at 09:50 (the deploy flushed the cache)? Can the page tolerate 30 s stale data?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Manually refill home:v3 before the next expiry with a script, and enable a circuit breaker so the DB caps concurrent aggregation at 20.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Stampede on expiry (matches identical queries); DB slowness (no, the same query copies prove a herd); deploy side effect that aligned expiry.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_activity grouped by query; Redis TTL home:v3; correlate the expiry timestamp with the spike.
  5. Root cause: At expiry, ~900 ms x 20,000/s = 18,000 requests miss and all run the 900 ms query. DB saturates, rebuild slows to seconds, and requests keep stacking.
  6. Fix: Single-flight: SET lock:home:v3 <id> NX PX 5000; the winner rebuilds, losers serve the stale copy (stored with a soft TTL inside the value) or sleep 50 ms plus jitter and retry. Also refresh this one key proactively every 5 min with a scheduled job.
  7. Prevention: A load test that expires the hot key; dashboard of "concurrent rebuilds per key".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a lock without a TTL (a crashed holder blocks the key forever), and I would not poll in a tight loop. Stale-while-revalidate costs a bit of freshness, acceptable for a home page.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Many app servers, one lock? -> Redis lock is global; also use in-process single-flight to cut Redis round trips.
  • Lock holder crashes? -> The PX 5000 expiry frees it; one more request rebuilds.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A daily 20-second slowdown was blamed on the DB for months; it was a single key with a 10-minute TTL refilled at an unlucky time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: raise TTL or scale DB.
  • Hire: single-flight lock with TTL and stale serving.
  • Strong hire: explains why it is aligned at 10:00, adds proactive refresh and DB-side protection.

questions.contextHtml: An API GET /orders/{id} sees a sudden 40,000 req/s. The legitimate rate is 2,000/s. Cache hit ratio drops to 5%; the DB shows 38,000 lookups/s returning zero rows. Requests come from 300 IPs with sequential-looking random 12-digit IDs. There are 100M valid order IDs. Redis memory is flat. Red herring: a marketing email went out an hour ago.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you stop it without breaking real users?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale up the DB and cache." Cache cannot help since the keys do not exist.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do the IDs follow a known format or checksum? Is the endpoint authenticated? Are the IPs a small ASN set? What is the cost of a false reject?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rate limit per IP and per ASN at the edge/WAF; block the 300 IPs; return 404 quickly.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Enumeration attack (random IDs, 0 rows); a buggy client retrying; a campaign link with a wrong ID format (check logs for a User-Agent).
  4. How I'd verify each: Group access logs by IP, UA, ID pattern; compare keyspace_misses with DB zero-row rate.
  5. Root cause: Penetration: nonexistent keys always miss and always hit the DB; nothing is ever cached.
  6. Fix: Layers: (a) ID format check (length, checksum) rejects most junk for free; (b) negative caching SET order:404:<id> 1 EX 60; (c) Bloom filter of valid IDs: 100M items at 1% FPR needs about 9.6 bits/item = 120 MB, so ~99% of junk dies in memory and about 380 req/s leak to the DB; (d) authentication and per-user rate limits.
  7. Prevention: Use non-guessable IDs (UUIDs or signed IDs); alert on zero-row ratio above a threshold.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A Bloom filter cannot delete and must learn new IDs: add on create, rebuild nightly. Negative TTL stays short, otherwise a newly created order looks missing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Newly created order gets a false 404? -> Add the ID to the Bloom filter and delete the negative key in the same create path.
  • 1% FPR too high at 40k/s? -> Use 0.1% (about 14.4 bits/item, 180 MB) or add rate limiting.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sequential-ID enumeration cost a company a weekend of DB alerts; the fix that stuck was opaque IDs plus the edge rate limit; the Bloom filter was a bonus.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales infrastructure.
  • Hire: negative cache, rate limit and Bloom filter.
  • Strong hire: does the filter sizing math, covers the creation race and recommends opaque IDs.

questions.contextHtml:
Every night at 02:00 a job warms the cache with 1.5M product keys. Exactly one hour after (03:00) the DB CPU goes to 100% for about 4 minutes, with 5,000 reads/s of misses vs the usual 300/s. Loader code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void warm(List<Product> all) {
    for (Product p : all) {
        redis.setex("p:" + p.id, 3600, serialize(p));   // same TTL for all
    }
}
fun warm(all: List<Product>) {
    all.forEach { redis.setex("p:${it.id}", 3600, serialize(it)) }   // same TTL for all
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and what would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the DB size." It ignores that the keys all expire inside the same minute.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How long does the warm job run (spread of insert times)? Is the data really invalid after 1 hour? Is there an in-process cache?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run a manual re-warm just before 03:00 with different TTLs, or rate-limit the DB path.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Same-TTL expiry cliff; job duration so short (about 2 minutes) that keys expire within the same window; a coincident cron on the DB.
  4. How I'd verify each: Histogram of key TTLs: redis-cli --scan | xargs TTL sampled; DB activity at 03:00; the job's duration.
  5. Root cause: Avalanche: 1.5M keys written within about 2 minutes with identical TTL expire within about 2 minutes. The 4-minute DB spike matches the expiry window plus rebuild queueing.
  6. Fix: ttl = 3600 + random(0, 600) per key; or TTL 24 h and event-driven invalidation; also add single-flight on rebuild and keep a small in-process cache.
  7. Prevention: A lint rule: no constant TTL in bulk loaders; a dashboard of expirations per minute (expired_keys rate).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not skip the TTL (stale forever on missed invalidation). Jitter widens the staleness bound by 10 minutes, which is fine here.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The cache node restarts at 03:00 anyway? -> Jitter does not help; need replicas and DB load shedding.
  • Why not set 24 h TTL only? -> Fine if invalidation is reliable; TTL is a safety net, not the mechanism.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "mysterious hourly outage" was a bulk loader with constant TTL; adding 10% jitter ended it in one deploy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale DB.
  • Hire: spots the identical TTL and adds jitter.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the window, adds layered caches and shedding, adds a lint rule.

questions.contextHtml: A team caches rendered HTML fragments (avg 40 KB) for a media site: 200 GB, 400,000 gets/s, no persistence needed, a plain get/set. They run on 32-core boxes. A second team wants a per-user rate limiter and a leaderboard on the same infrastructure. The CTO asks "Memcached or Redis?" and wants one answer.
questions.promptHtml: What do you recommend and why? Is it a reversible decision?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Redis is faster / more popular." No workload reasoning.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Failure tolerance if a node loses everything? Do we need replication/HA? Value sizes and growth? Ops skills and managed-service options?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Fragments: pure get/set at high throughput, multi-core fits Memcached; rate limiter and leaderboard need atomic counters and sorted sets: Redis.
  4. How I'd verify each: Benchmark both with real value sizes (memtier_benchmark) on the target hardware; check CPU per node at 400k gets/s.
  5. Root cause / reasoning: Memcached is multi-threaded so one 32-core node can serve high gets/s with low per-key overhead. Redis executes commands on a single thread (I/O threads help since 6.0), so you need more processes or shards for the same throughput. Redis brings data structures: ZADD/ZREVRANGE for leaderboards, INCR+EXPIRE or Lua for rate limits.
  6. Fix / recommendation: Two systems for two jobs is acceptable: Memcached (or Redis behind a get/set interface) for fragments; Redis for counters and leaderboards. If the org wants one platform, Redis for operational simplicity and HA, accepting more nodes for the fragment tier.
  7. Prevention: Hide the cache behind an interface (get/set/delete) so the choice stays reversible.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use Redis as a durable store without understanding AOF everysec can lose about 1 s. Memcached has no built-in replication or failover, so a node loss means a cold shard.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fragment value grows to 1 MB? -> Both handle it but big values block Redis; reconsider chunking or a CDN.
  • Need HA for fragments? -> Redis replicas, or multiple Memcached pools with client-side failover.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team standardized on Redis for everything and later needed 3x the nodes for a pure-get tier; a get/set interface made the split a config change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one by popularity.
  • Hire: matches features to workload (threads, data types, HA).
  • Strong hire: benchmarks, hides behind an interface, and states reversibility.

questions.promptHtml: What are hot keys and big keys in a sharded Redis, why does adding nodes not fix them, and how do you find and mitigate each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that sharding splits the key space, not a single key, and Redis' single-threaded execution.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A hot key gets more traffic than one node can serve; hashing pins it to one shard, so more nodes do not help. A big key is one huge value (a list with millions of entries) whose commands block the single-threaded event loop. For hot keys I add a local in-process cache or split the key into copies; for big keys I split into buckets and use UNLINK. I detect both with --hotkeys/--bigkeys and client metrics.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
One Redis node does about 100k simple ops/s (hardware dependent). A key at 300k reads/s saturates its owner while others idle. Mitigations:

local cache 1s TTL  -> Redis load for that key ~ N_servers per second
key copies          -> profile:42#0..#9, read random, write all 10
read replicas       -> reads spread, with staleness

Big keys: DEL on a 5M-entry list blocks for hundreds of ms; UNLINK frees in the background. Cluster MIGRATE of a big key also stalls. Detection: redis-cli --bigkeys (scans), --hotkeys (requires LFU policy), MEMORY USAGE, SLOWLOG GET.

redis-cli --hotkeys
redis-cli --bigkeys
redis-cli UNLINK big:list

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Add more shards" for a single hot key.
  • KEYS * or DEL of a huge key in production.
  • Key copies without a plan for updating all copies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is a 1 s local TTL so effective? -> With 50 app servers, Redis sees at most 50 reads/s for that key instead of 300,000.
  2. Cost of key copies? -> Writes fan out to N copies and may be briefly inconsistent.
  3. Redis hot slot from a hash tag? -> Same issue: one slot, one node; use finer tags.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "shard more". Senior: explains key-to-node pinning, local caches, copies and the blocking nature of big keys.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A celebrity profile took one shard to 100% CPU during a live event while the rest sat idle.

questions.promptHtml: Can you treat Redis as a durable store? What can be lost on a crash or a failover?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know Redis persistence and async replication from those who treat it as a database.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Not by default. RDB snapshots lose everything since the last snapshot. AOF with appendfsync everysec loses up to about one second; always loses almost nothing but is slow. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose acknowledged writes that did not reach the replica. Good for caches and ephemeral state; for data I cannot lose I write to a real DB first.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RDB       fork + snapshot every N min   loss: minutes
AOF       append every write            everysec: ~1s, always: ~0, no: OS decides
Replica   async stream                  loss: unreplicated tail on failover
WAIT n t  blocks until n replicas ack    reduces, does not eliminate, loss

Fork for RDB/AOF rewrite uses copy-on-write: heavy writes during a snapshot can nearly double memory, hence maxmemory at 60-75% of RAM. Memcached has none of this: loss on restart is total, which is fine for a cache.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec
min-replicas-to-write 1
min-replicas-max-lag 10

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling everysec durable.
  • Believing Sentinel or Cluster failover is lossless.
  • Running snapshots with no memory headroom.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does WAIT make it strongly consistent? -> No; it only confirms replica receipt at that moment, and a promoted replica could still be a different one.
  2. Where is Redis-as-primary acceptable? -> Rebuildable data, rate-limit counters, presence, sessions with re-login fallback.
  3. What would you use for money? -> A transactional DB, with Redis only as a cache.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Redis has AOF so it is durable". Senior: gives the loss window of each mode and the failover gap, and keeps the source of truth elsewhere.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a failover, a team's idempotency keys in Redis were gone and duplicate charges were attempted; the keys needed a DB-backed unique constraint.

questions.contextHtml: A social app runs a 10-shard Redis Cluster at about 40,000 ops/s per shard. During a live event, one celebrity profile key profile:777 jumps to 300,000 reads/s. Shard 4 shows 100% CPU, p99 latency 900 ms, connected_clients climbing; the other 9 shards are at 25% CPU. App servers: 60. The profile JSON is 3 KB and changes about once per hour. Red herring: network is fine (shard 4 NIC at 40% utilisation).
questions.promptHtml: Mitigate now, and design the fix for good.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more shards" or "upgrade the node". Neither splits one key.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the profile be a second stale? Are the reads from app servers or from a mobile client directly? How many other keys are hot? Are there writes to this key?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a 1-2 s in-process cache for this key via a feature flag; or push the profile to the CDN with max-age=5.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Single hot key (matches one shard hot); big key (3 KB: no); client hot loop/retry storm (check connection count growth).
  4. How I'd verify each: redis-cli -h shard4 --hotkeys (with LFU) or MONITOR sampled for 3 s (briefly, it is costly); SLOWLOG; app metrics on top keys.
  5. Root cause: Slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384 maps profile:777 to shard 4. Single-threaded execution at about 100k ops/s serialises the 300k/s.
  6. Fix: Short term: local cache. Long term: automatic hot-key detection in the client library (sliding counters) that promotes keys over a threshold into a local cache with TTL 1-2 s; replicate the key as profile:777#0..#9 for the rest; or serve celebrities from the CDN.
  7. Prevention: Load test with a Zipf (power-law) distribution; alert on per-shard ops skew above 3x.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: With 60 servers and a 1 s TTL, Redis sees at most 60 reads/s for the key (99.98% reduction). The cost: up to 1 s staleness. I would not rebalance slots, since one key cannot be split.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Profile edit must show immediately for the owner? -> Bypass the local cache for the owner's own reads.
  • 10 hot keys now? -> Same mechanism, automated detection and an LRU-bounded local cache.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A product launch livestream saturated one shard; resharding had no effect, and a 1-second in-process cache fixed it in an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: add shards.
  • Hire: local cache or key replication with correct reasoning.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the load reduction, detection automation, owner-read consistency and skew alerts.

questions.contextHtml: You must move a 180 GB single-primary Redis (about 90k ops/s, maxed at 85% CPU) to Redis Cluster. Code uses MGET, a Lua script reserve_stock.lua touching stock:{sku} and reserved:{sku}, and SUNIONSTORE across user sets. The test cluster returns: (error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot. The product owner wants zero downtime.
questions.promptHtml: What is your plan and what do you change in the key design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just point the client at the cluster." It ignores CROSSSLOT and slot-based design.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which commands are multi-key, how frequent? Is data rebuildable or durable? Is the client cluster-aware? Tolerance for a short write pause?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No incident; keep the old node serving while preparing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Multi-key ops fail across slots; hash tags can fix some but create hot slots; client lacks cluster support; resharding needs balanced slots.
  4. How I'd verify each: Grep code and SLOWLOG for multi-key commands; CLUSTER KEYSLOT for sample keys; staging replay of production traffic.
  5. Root cause: Cluster routes by slot; commands on keys in different slots cannot run atomically on one node.
  6. Fix: Rename keys stock:{sku} and reserved:{sku} so the tag {sku} co-locates them (Lua then works). Replace MGET with a pipeline, grouped per slot by the client library. SUNIONSTORE across users: compute in the app or restructure so it works per user tag. Migration: dual-write to both clusters, backfill with scan plus MIGRATE/replication tool, verify with checksums on samples, shift reads by percentage, then writes, and keep the old node for rollback.
  7. Prevention: Key-design review rule: every multi-key op declares its tag; tests run against a cluster in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not tag everything with one tenant ID: one slot (max 1/16,384 of space) becomes the hot node. Dual-write has a consistency gap; for rebuildable data it is acceptable, for counters I would freeze writes briefly and reconcile.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The {sku} tag turns hot for one bestseller? -> That SKU is a hot key; apply hot-key mitigations and consider moving its stock check to a DB row lock or a queue.
  • Failover loses writes? -> Async replication; keep stock reservations backed by the DB.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team cut over and discovered CROSSSLOT in production because staging was a single node; running CI on a 3-node cluster would have caught it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: direct cutover.
  • Hire: hash tags and dual-write migration.
  • Strong hire: addresses hot slots, replication loss and CI against a real cluster.

questions.contextHtml: At 19:12 one of 3 Redis cluster masters crashes and its replica is also lost (both on the same rack). Slots 5461-10922 (a third of the key space) are empty after a restart at 19:14. App p99 goes 30 ms -> 4 s; DB connection pool exhausted (FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved); error rate 18%. Metrics: DB QPS jumped from 800 to 9,000; the DB limit is about 3,000. Traffic is 30,000 reads/s.
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the first 15 minutes and the long-term fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the app servers" (adds more cold traffic) or "scale the DB" which takes 30 minutes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the DB the failing layer (yes, connection pool)? Are errors user-visible on read paths only? Can we serve stale or degrade features? What is the per-shard hit ratio now?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load: lower the DB pool timeout and cap concurrent DB queries per instance; enable stale/default responses for non-critical endpoints (recommendations, counters); rate limit low-priority clients; keep app servers running.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Cold third of the cache sends ~10k/s misses extra (9,000 vs 800 matches); no single-flight, so hot keys stampede; retry storm in clients.
  4. How I'd verify each: redis-cli --cluster check, CLUSTER NODES; DB pg_stat_activity; client retry metrics.
  5. Root cause: Avalanche by node loss with no layered cache and a DB without shedding; replica on the same rack gave no real redundancy.
  6. Fix: Short term: warm hot keys through a script (top 10k keys by recent access) while shedding. Long term: a 30 s in-process L1 cache; single-flight; replicas in different failure domains; DB circuit breaker; a warm standby; failover tests.
  7. Prevention: Game day: kill a shard at peak; alert on DB QPS vs capacity; SLO for degraded mode.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not flush the rest of the cache to "sync". Serving stale data costs correctness on some views, buys DB survival.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Retries from the mobile app double the load? -> Exponential backoff with jitter; server returns Retry-After.
  • The replica did take over but data was missing? -> Async replication lost a tail; for a cache that is fine.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Replica and primary shared a power feed; the failover "worked" on paper and the cache lost both. The postmortem moved replicas across zones.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts things; scales slowly.
  • Hire: sheds load, warms hot keys, adds L1 and replicas.
  • Strong hire: quantifies miss load vs DB limit, covers failure domains, retry storms and drills.

questions.contextHtml:
You review a stampede fix. After deploy, once a week a key report:daily returns 503 for about 5 minutes until someone deletes lock:report:daily by hand. Code:

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
String get(String key) {
    String v = redis.get(key);
    if (v != null) return v;
    if (redis.setnx("lock:" + key, "1") == 1) {   // acquire
        v = loadFromDb(key);                      // can take 20 s or throw
        redis.set(key, v, 600);
        redis.del("lock:" + key);                 // release
        return v;
    }
    while (redis.get(key) == null) { }            // wait
    return redis.get(key);
}
fun get(key: String): String {
    redis.get(key)?.let { return it }
    if (redis.setnx("lock:$key", "1") == 1L) {   // acquire
        val v = loadFromDb(key)                  // can take 20 s or throw
        redis.set(key, v, 600)
        redis.del("lock:$key")                   // release
        return v
    }
    while (redis.get(key) == null) { }           // wait
    return redis.get(key)!!
}
questions.promptHtml: List the bugs and give a corrected version.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a try/catch." It misses the missing lock TTL, the busy loop and the unsafe unlock.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Max load time? How many app instances? Can we serve stale data? Is Redis a single node or cluster (lock safety)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Delete the stuck lock; set a short TTL on any lock keys found without one (TTL returns -1).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lock never released when loadFromDb throws or the process dies; (b) busy-wait loop burns CPU and hammers Redis; (c) release by plain DEL can delete someone else's lock after expiry.
  4. How I'd verify each: redis-cli TTL lock:report:daily is -1; app thread dump shows spinning loops; DB logs show a timed-out query that same time.
  5. Root cause: SETNX without expiry plus no finally: a failure leaves the lock forever, and waiters spin until the 503.
  6. Fix: SET lock:key <uuid> NX PX 30000; try/finally; release with a compare-and-delete Lua script (delete only if the value equals my uuid); waiters sleep 50 ms plus jitter with a bounded deadline and then serve stale data stored under key:stale, else fail fast; also keep a soft TTL inside the value to refresh early.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test: kill the loader mid-rebuild; a lint rule against SETNX without PX; metrics on lock hold time.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A Redis lock is advisory and not a correctness guarantee (clock pauses, failover); for a cache rebuild that is fine since duplicates only cost work. I would not use it for a money critical section.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Load takes longer than the lock TTL? -> Another loader starts: acceptable duplicate work; or extend the lock with a heartbeat.
  • Redis is down? -> Fall back to a per-process single-flight so each server runs one rebuild.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A weekly 503 was a lock that outlived a crashed worker; the one-line PX would have prevented months of manual deletes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only adds try/catch.
  • Hire: finds the missing TTL, busy loop and unsafe unlock.
  • Strong hire: writes the owner-checked release, serves stale, and states the limits of Redis locks.
